Astronomical observations through the Very Large Telescope's VLT/UVES spectrograph are compromised by the effects of atmospheric dispersion, which can be quantified and measured to evaluate the equipment's performance and develop suitable correction techniques. By analyzing the dispersion curve, researchers can determine the level of distortion affecting the spectrograph's resolution. To achieve this, a new method utilizing VLT/UVES itself is introduced, which involves analyzing wavelength calibration spectra. By comparing these spectra to theoretical models, the dispersion curve can be calculated. To enhance the reliability of this measurement, the theoretical models are refined by characterizing the atmospheric dispersion model and its uncertainty, which is achieved through numerical simulations. By combining this model with a likelihood function, researchers can determine the parameters of the dispersion curve and its uncertainty. The results of this study show that the dispersion curve can be measured with high precision, with an uncertainty of approximately 0.00003, which is comparable to the uncertainty of the theoretical models used.

This study introduces a novel Bayesian method for the robust modeling of multiple time series, drawing on the strengths of the Deep Variational Information Maximization (DIVAM) model. The proposed approach combines two key elements: (1) a pre-trained deep generative model, trained on a large collection of time series, and (2) the application of a Bayesian framework to incorporate sparsity and transfer learning. By utilizing Bayesian divergence as a measure of information, our method effectively captures the underlying patterns in time series data while filtering out noise. Furthermore, it can be seamlessly extended to accommodate various types of missing data and missing-not-at-random scenarios. Our method's performance is rigorously evaluated through its ability to predict stock prices and its capacity to detect time series in the human gait cycle.

In a setting of continuous logic, Pontryagin duality can be extended to a broader context, specifically to closed, abelian groups that utilize a metric based on the distance function d(x,y) = min{|x-y|,1}. This extension is exemplified through a new proof of a fundamental theorem, stating that any countable, mixed, finite permutation group can be represented as a continuous logic structure, achieved by viewing such groups as subgroups of the group of automorphisms of an infinite set equipped with the discrete topology. As an added benefit, this approach yields a straightforward proof of the duality theorem for discrete groups.

This work explores the application of federated learning (FL) in promoting fairness and data protection. It delves into the unique aspects of FL that make it a suitable framework for achieving both goals. Furthermore, fairness and privacy are defined in both global and local contexts. The paper also compares the suitability of two optimization algorithms, stochastic gradient descent and adaptive moment estimation, for maintaining a balanced and private federated model.

In the supersymmetric standard model, a new $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry is introduced to resolve the dark matter issue. By incorporating it into the R-parity violating standard model, a right-handed neutrino, specifically $\nu_e^c$, is suggested as a dark matter candidate. A $U(1)_X$ gauge interaction is then considered as a mediator for this particle. To ensure the stability of $\nu_e^c$ as a dark matter particle, it is assumed that the $U(1)_X$ symmetry is not broken by any vacuum expectation value. Furthermore, it is assumed that the $U(1)_X$ symmetry is broken at the energy scale of a few TeV. A detailed analysis of the constraints on the $Z^\prime$ boson's couplings to standard model particles is conducted within the supersymmetric framework, considering the $U(1)_X$ symmetry's parameters. A specific parameter space is identified where the $Z^\prime$ boson can be a viable explanation for the dark matter density in the universe.

In our research, we examine a smart reflective surface-aided wireless-powered network where a single transmitter provides power to multiple energy-harvesting receivers and data receivers, each transmitting back to the transmitter with single-carrier signals. The presence of reflective surfaces in this communication system significantly impacts performance by reflecting interference at the receivers. To optimize throughput, we develop an algorithm that simultaneously determines the reflective surfaces' surface current density, power allocation, and transmission beamforming for the multi-hop process. A key limitation in this communication system is the complexity of jointly optimizing the reflective surfaces' parameters, power, and beamforming. To address this, we employ a deep learning approach that incorporates unsupervised learning to minimize the effect of interference and maximize throughput by training the model with synthetic data and applying it to real-world scenarios.

The study of the $^{186}$Hg isotope's properties is of great interest for understanding the nuclear structure of Hg isotopes near the minimum of the neutron shell. Researchers at the GSI National Laboratory in Darmstadt, Germany, conducted an experiment to study the β-decay properties of highly neutron-rich $^{186}$Hg. Using the ISOLDE facility at CERN, the isotope was produced and implanted into a silicon detector, where its β-decay properties were measured. The results showed that the half-life of $^{186}$Hg is 2.7(2) seconds, and the study revealed that the β-decay is dominated by transitions to the ground state and a low-lying excited state in the parent nucleus. The study also found that the low-lying states in $^{186}$Hg have a significant octupole character, which is consistent with predictions made by theoretical models. The study's findings have important implications for understanding the structure of Hg isotopes and the behavior of neutron-rich nuclei.

We explore the relationship between dark matter and leptogenesis within a unified framework based on a three-Higgs doublet model. In this framework, dark matter is composed of a pair of charged fermions, whose stability is ensured by a discrete $Z_2$ symmetry. The same fermions serve as intermediaries in the process of generating cosmic baryon asymmetry, while their annihilation process is further influenced by trilinear couplings involving the additional Higgs doublets. These fermions, being electrically charged, are also examined in the context of future collider experiments, such as the Large Hadron Collider and the High-Luminosity LHC, as well as their detection by fixed-target experiments, like the Dark Matter Search at Intensity Frontier.

This study introduces a novel control approach, known as LARS, which leverages
Reinforcement Learning to develop controllers capable of mastering multiple tasks.
LARS operates by training a single controller to accomplish a variety of objectives,
such as navigating a simulation environment, and it does so by employing a unique
side information system that mimics traditional control methods. To optimize its
performance, LARS employs a combination of exploration and exploitation strategies,
and it also employs a reward function that encourages the controller to adapt its
behavior based on the specific task at hand. Through simulations of both digital
and physical systems, this research demonstrates the effectiveness of LARS in 
producing robust controllers that can perform multiple tasks efficiently, even 
with limited data available for training.

We examine the complex plane representation of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory, utilizing primary fields $\Phi_{n_1,n_2}(z,\bar{z})$ governed by two-dimensional Ward identities. These identities facilitate the computation of multi-point correlation functions through the solution of partial differential equations, as demonstrated in the case of four-point functions. Our approach yields results that align with the results derived from the global conformal symmetry of the correlators.

Despite advancements in generating realistic images using GANs, a significant challenge remains in creating synthetic objects with predefined properties, particularly when the desired characteristics are defined by relationships. To address this shortcoming, we introduce the concept of tripling GANs, which utilizes latent relationships to produce visual content. To this end, we develop a method for relation learning, which enables the formation of relationships between a pair of images, and combine this with relation networks to generate visual content that mirrors the desired characteristics. To further solidify the relation between generated images and real images, we devise an innovative loss function, triplet loss, which complements traditional adversarial losses. Through extensive experimentation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in relation learning and its potential for generating high-quality synthetic objects with defined characteristics.

The typical quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol's key generation rate is often restricted by the distance due to photon loss. To overcome this problem, the typical-subset method faces distance limitations, the twin-field QKD protocol has been developed to achieve better performance. However, existing TF-QKD protocols require precise phase locking between the Alice and Bob signals, which poses a significant challenge for long-distance communication. In this study, we present a modified TF-QKD protocol that eliminates the need for phase locking, thereby simplifying the implementation. Our results show that the proposed protocol outperforms typical-subset QKD and is comparable to TF-QKD with phase locking while maintaining a similar key consumption rate.

Let H be a Hilbert space and let B(H) denote the set of bounded linear operators acting on H. This note delves into a specific class of operators within B(H), focusing on Toeplitz operators. These are operator pairs (T_g, T_{\bar{g}}) derived from functions (g) belonging to either the Hardy space or the Bergman space over the unit disk. The study aims to categorize and understand the algebraic structure formed by (T_g, T_{\bar{g}}) in B(H), specifically with g in either the Hardy or Bergman space, and further identifies conditions under which this (T_g, T_{\bar{g}}) forms a subalgebra within B(H).

Detecting uncommon and rare items in vast visual domains poses a significant challenge for object detection. To tackle this issue, open-vocabulary object detection has emerged as an effective solution, relying on pre-trained language models to identify items beyond the scope of training-time data. However, current approaches often suffer from the limitations of noisy training labels, which hinders their performance. To mitigate this problem, we introduce a novel pseudo labeling method, called P2LB, that effectively leverages text-to-image models to minimize the impact of noise. By using this method, we achieve substantial performance improvements across various scenarios. Our proposed framework, P2LB, outperforms existing solutions on MS-COCO and FAIR-101 datasets, yielding notable gains in top-K average precision metrics. Furthermore, we make our code and pre-trained models available to the public to facilitate further research and development in this area.

The S1 ionization complex, a striking feature in the Rho Ophiuchus molecular cloud, is primarily illuminated by the T Tauri star S1. A key aspect of understanding this area involves comprehending the role of photodissociation regions (PDRs) - where ionized, atomic, and molecular gas interact. This study presents new findings from a high-resolution study of the S1 area, revealing that the primary branch of the S1 complex, S1A, is a collection of PDRs. It also reveals that S1A is connected to a region of ionized gas, S1B, by a thin layer of PDRs. These results indicate that S1A's formation is linked to the presence of the PDRs.

The remarkable success of Transformer models in natural language processing tasks has piqued the interest of computer vision researchers, leading to a surge in applications of Transformer-based architectures in vision tasks. Despite a comprehensive overview of Transformer models' capabilities in NLP, there remains a lack of extensive surveys on their capabilities in vision tasks. This paper aims to fill this gap by providing an extensive survey of key vision tasks and the application of Transformer models within them. The focus is on highlighting the unique advantages of Transformers over traditional convolutional neural networks in various vision tasks, as well as identifying the limitations of current research and suggesting future directions for improvement.

Mortality forecasting models based on standard factor analysis have shown promising results, but the assumption of time-invariant factor loadings may not accurately capture the complex nature of time series data. A more realistic approach would be to allow factor loadings to change over time, and this study compares the performance of factor models with time-varying and time-invariant factor loadings using a data-driven and Bayesian shrinkage method. A simulation experiment and an empirical analysis of US and Italian mortality data demonstrate that factormodels with time-varying factor loadings can provide a more accurate and reliable forecasting performance, especially in situations where time-varying factor loadings are present.

Research into Neural Architecture Search, NNS, has led to the creation of numerous network architectures that excel on various tasks. The primary focus of most existing methods is on optimizing individual tasks, whereas this paper explores the potential for improving multiple tasks simultaneously. The study examines how a single search can be utilized to address several related tasks, such as learning representations for image and text comprehension. The results demonstrate that a joint NNS on these tasks yields superior outcomes on a range of benchmarks compared to optimizing these tasks separately. The paper also identifies key factors contributing to the success of this approach and suggests potential avenues for future research.

Time series analysis is a crucial aspect of statistical analysis, and its significance is amplified by the ease of access to data and the advent of automated monitoring systems. However, the time series analysis community has been somewhat limited by the availability of comprehensive software tools. In response to this need, the theft package has been developed, offering a powerful R-based platform for extracting meaningful characteristics from multivariate time series data. This paper presents an overview of the main features of the theft package, highlighting its built-in univariate and multivariate feature extraction functions, the ability to calculate rolling statistics, and the inclusion of over 100 pre-defined operators. Additionally, the document showcases the utility of the integrated multivariate time series similarity search and outlier detection modules, as well as the visualization tools provided within the package.
We identify concrete, infinitely precise criteria under which a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space has a semistable fundamental group at its boundary.

Human-assisted translation is a crucial component of the translation process, and its effectiveness relies heavily on thorough quality control measures. To improve this control, we utilize a Bayesian inference-based approach, which calculates the probability of a translator's accuracy. By treating this probability as a random variable influenced by various factors, we can estimate it using existing translator reliability data and then apply this knowledge to new scenarios. Our methodology involves conducting a series of experiments to validate its effectiveness in different contexts.

In general scattering scenarios, there's a specific subsystem interacting with a broad, featureless environment. In the context of two-level systems coupled to a bath, certain directions of excitation, known as eigenchannels, become decoupled from the bath and remain unaffected. In this paper, we focus on the decay rates and final states associated with these eigenchannels. By summing over all possible initial states, we obtain sum rules that relate average decay rates to key properties of the subsystem-bath interaction. These relationships provide valuable insights into unresolved properties of eigenchannels, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of their behavior.

Deep neural networks have become the go-to choice for solving complex tasks due to their impressive performance. Despite their success, questions remain about their internal workings and the specific factors that contribute to their performance. To investigate this, we conducted a study on the effectiveness of pruning techniques, which remove unnecessary network components to reduce computation and memory requirements. Our results show that pruning fully connected networks significantly impacts their performance, but the same does not happen with pruning convolutional networks. This suggests that the specific structure of convolutional networks helps them retain their performance even after removing unnecessary components. To further explore this phenomenon, we developed a new pruning method that automatically determines the best network configuration for a given task, and the performance of this method matches that of existing state-of-the-art methods, but with fewer network parameters and a smaller size.

In the realm of sports betting, "correct score" wagers are renowned for their
lucrative potential, albeit with significant risk. A unique strategy to
capitalize on these bets involves the shared ownership model, allowing owners to
collect winnings while dividing the cost, thus maximizing expected returns.
In this paper, we investigate the optimal strategy for selling and purchasing
these bets, with a focus on their overall value. Through our developed model,
which accounts for factors such as team popularity, team performance, and the
betting cycle, we demonstrate that successful bet sharing requires the early
sale of bets shortly after the game's announcement, with remaining bets
purchased closer to the game date. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the
expected value of shared bets can be up to 100% higher than their traditional
counterparts.

The most basic operator $\phi^Q$ within the $O(N)$-symmetric $\lambda\phi^Q$ theory is studied, where $Q$ is an integer. The six-loop anomalous dimension of this operator is computed in the massless theory using the $\epsilon$ expansion to two-loop order in terms of the basic six-loop value. This results in a comprehensive formula for the anomalous dimension $\gamma_{\phi^Q}(d, N, \lambda)$, with the known five-dimensional and four-dimensional values as inputs.

In two-dimensional materials, valley properties play a crucial role, but conventional electron-phonon interactions have limited effects in certain cases. New electron-phonon mechanisms, however, significantly enhance these couplings by several orders of magnitude, giving rise to a wide range of exciting phenomena. These novel mechanisms involve interactions between electrons and phonons that generate light, light-induced valley mixing, and even unconventional valley textures. The latter exhibits phonon-induced valley-dependent curvature in momentum space, leading to valley-dependent phonon scattering and sound propagation. The impact of these mechanisms can be observed in valley-dependent transport, sound propagation, and even in the creation of new types of light-matter hybridized states.

The Visual Domain Adaptation challenge of NeurIPS 2022 involves adapting a source dataset to a target dataset across various semantic categories without direct access to target images or labels. This study presents a new method called Heterogeneous Graph Neural Code Adaptation (HGNC), which achieves superior results on the challenge. HGNC comprises two key components: Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network Code (HGNNC) and Semi-Supervised Hyper-Contrastive Learning (SSLHCL). HGNNC transforms source and target features into a unified semantic space using a sophisticated graph-based approach, allowing for more accurate code representation. Subsequently, a semi-supervised contrastive learning approach (SSLHCL) is employed to refine the HGNNC-generated codes using both labeled source data and a small set of target labels. This method successfully outperforms existing solutions, achieving a mean Average Precision of 62.1% on the challenge dataset.

t-SNE is a widely used technique for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its underlying assumption, however, relies on a Euclidean distance space, neglecting the potential benefits of other space models. This work introduces VMF-SNE, a novel t-SNE variant that incorporates the properties of the spherical data space. By adapting the original algorithm to work with the Wishart distribution on the Stiefel manifold, VMF-SNE enables the exploration of data in non-Euclidean space while maintaining the computational efficiency of the original method. Experimental results demonstrate that VMF-SNE produces superior embeddings compared to other approaches, including its Euclidean counterpart.

The two-dimensional non-degenerate Fermi polaron, where a bosonic impurity interacts with a Fermi sea of bosonic or fermionic particles, is examined using a novel diagrammatic Monte Carlo approach. This method enables the calculation of the polaron's binding energy and the self-energy through the summation of Feynman diagrams in the particle-hole and rainbow topologies. A critical issue identified in this study is the presence of divergences in these topologies, which are shown to be indicative of a diagrammatic cancellation problem. Furthermore, the results indicate that the binding energy of the polaron is independent of the scattering length's sign, and the dependence of the binding energy on mass ratio is consistent with Monte Carlo simulations in the bosonic and classical limits. A notable feature of the self-energy is the emergence of a branch cut, which is consistent with the expected behavior of the polaron's pole.

We have developed an end-to-end demonstration of a quantum simulation for fermionic systems, which can be applied to quantum chemistry and high-energy physics, using a hybrid digital-analog approach. Our results show that by incorporating digital operations to correct analog noise in the quantum processor, we can significantly enhance the accuracy of simulations. We observed that the outcomes of our simulations were in good agreement with the experiment on IBM's quantum computer, particularly when the coupling strengths were small, less than 0.1, and the coupling was sufficiently weak, less than 0.5, the simulations were able to reproduce the exact analytical solutions. Our research highlights the potential of the hybrid digital-analog approach as a promising pathway for large-scale quantum simulations.

A class of graphs, with a fixed number of vertices and edges, has a corresponding sequence of polynomials derived from a combinatorial formula. This formula's components are shown to correspond to specific graph characteristics, including the graph's cycles and their orientations. The limit of this polynomial sequence can be determined as a function of the graphs' cycle lengths. The theorem generalizes previous findings by Guo and Klivans, who had a restricted set of variables in their polynomial formula.

We demonstrate that as Ascoli's family of translation surfaces approaches a Veech surface, the Hitchin connection converges to a holomorphic line bundle constructed by Aschi and Mellit. This implies that the Hitchin connection defines a flat line bundle. Additionally, we confirm that this flat bundle is a key component in the monodromy representation developed by Aschi and Mellit.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused significant disruptions to the global economy, prompting governments to enforce lockdowns and work-from-home policies. These measures have had a profound impact on software developers, who have had to adapt to remote work environments.  In this study, we investigate the effects of working from home on the performance of software teams, who have had to rely on remote collaboration tools.  Our research reveals that working from home poses significant challenges to software teams, who have had to adjust their communication and collaboration strategies.  In particular, we found that the shift to remote work has had a negative impact on the productivity of Scrum teams, who have had to adapt their agile practices to suit remote collaboration.  To address these challenges, we propose that Scrum teams should focus on improving their remote collaboration skills, using video conferencing tools, and adopting agile practices that are suitable for remote work.  These findings have significant implications for software teams, who have had to adapt to remote work environments, and highlight the need for agile practices to be re-evaluated in light of remote collaboration.

The concept of the Gau-Wu number originates from a particular entry in the inverse of a positive definite matrix, specifically a unit diagonal entry. This entry is shown to depend on a determinant involving the lower left submatrix of the given matrix. The Gau-Wu number finds application in a variety of fields, including multivariate statistics and combinatorics. Researchers have developed recursive formulas to determine the Gau-Wu number for arrowhead matrices, and in this paper, we derive the Gau-Wu number for a $4 \times 4$ symmetric positive definite matrix in closed form. Additionally, we explore some interesting properties of the Gau-Wu number for arrowhead matrices.

In high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC, the transverse momentum distribution of elliptic flow for specific momentum ranges (1-6 GeV/c) is studied through beauty-hadron decays at a luminosity of $3~{\rm nb}^{-1}$. This research reveals a distinct $v_2$ pattern for beauty-hadron leptons, which correlates with their corresponding hadronic counterparts. This observation suggests that beauty hadrons are formed within the collision environment and that $v_2$ generated during their formation is preserved. This outcome is consistent with a thermal model, which provides a temperature estimate of approximately 155 MeV.

In the field of data analysis, topological methods have gained significant traction, particularly in understanding complex relationships within high-dimensional data sets. The alpha complex, a crucial concept in this context, has been widely applied to solve various problems. However, it has limitations, as it only captures one dimension of information. To address this, researchers have developed the chromatic alpha complex, which leverages the full potential of this method by incorporating multi-scale color information. The main goal of this study is to explore the topological characteristics of the chromatic alpha complex through the use of persistent homology. The findings reveal that the complex exhibits a rich structure, encompassing features spanning various scales. The study further demonstrates that the chromatic alpha complex outperforms its single-colored counterpart in capturing essential traits of underlying point clouds.

This work investigates the performance difference between optimal power control and equalized power control in terms of the spatial gain, specifically in a scenario with an arbitrary number of users and transmitters. Optimal power control maximizes the total network throughput, while equalized power control allocates the same amount of power to all users. Notably, in networks with multiple antennas, the spatial gain difference between these two controls can be substantial, with a substantial analytical and numerical analysis conducted to demonstrate this disparity.

Auditing processes can be time-consuming and labor-intensive, particularly in the age of big data, where traditional methods often prove insufficient. To address this issue, we utilize formal concept analysis and the Dempster-Shafer theory to create a flexible categorization framework for auditing. This approach enables the use of vague and imprecise data, which is frequently encountered in auditing contexts, by assigning degrees of membership to objects within concept nodes rather than strict binary classifications. Furthermore, the proposed framework allows for the incorporation of partial information and varying levels of confidence, which is particularly beneficial when dealing with incomplete datasets. To further enhance its utility, we develop an algorithm for automatically generating dendro-concepts, which serve as potential classifications and can be assigned confidence degrees. This methodology is successfully applied to a real-world dataset, thereby demonstrating its effectiveness in auditing applications.

The Strauss process is a point process, which can be thought of as a constrained version of a Poisson process, where nearby points are discouraged from appearing together. This process has been linked to a wide range of phenomena, including the distribution of galaxies, the placement of buildings in a city, and the structure of a random Voronoi tessellation. In this study, a new method for generating samples from the Strauss distribution is introduced, which is based on a concept known as stitching, which allows for the combination of independent processes to create a process with desired intensity and restriction properties.

In this study, we examine how the Generalized Uncertainty Principle impacts particle motion and the symmetry groups governing space-time, specifically the Lorentz group and the Galilean group. Our analysis reveals that the Generalized Uncertainty Principle yields two possible corrections, each incorporating a single length-scale, that significantly impact motion at both large and small scales. The first correction, applicable to laboratory settings, aligns with the Planck length and is characterized by a length-scale that asymptotically approaches infinity. Conversely, the second, more relevant to small scales, incorporates a length parameter that diminishes towards infinity and is driven by a length-scale that tends towards zero. Our work demonstrates that the generalization of the uncertainty principle leads to novel finite representations of the symmetry groups and the emergence of a minimal length, thereby resolving the issue of space-time singularities. Furthermore, we show that the first-order GUP corrections yield a novel formulation of space-time transformation, encompassing a length, time, and velocity, that maintains the fundamental principle of relativity.

We've developed a new model called Multitasking Scheduling with Shared Processing, where the primary difference from traditional scheduling problems is that a fraction of the jobs can be performed concurrently on a single machine, while the rest must be done individually. The goal in this model is to minimize the makespan, which is the total time required to complete all the jobs. Our research provides a comprehensive analysis of the model, showing that it is strongly NP-hard and offers both approximation algorithms and inapproximability results for various versions of the problem. Additionally, we've proven that certain scenarios involving a small number of jobs are computationally difficult to solve, while also establishing lower bounds on the approximation ratio for polynomial-time algorithms.

A sophisticated simulation model has been developed to accurately represent the behavior of a monopod robot navigating soft terrain. The monopod's dynamics are based on the principles of a point-foot hopper, while the ground is modeled as a layered medium consisting of an elastic top layer over a rigid base. To validate the model, a high-fidelity simulation model was created, combining monopod dynamics with a complex terrain representation. The model was then applied to optimize monopod parameters using a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm. To assess the accuracy of the optimized model, the simulation results were compared to those of a model assuming hard ground, revealing notable differences. The optimized monopod's performance was also evaluated by analyzing changes in its oscillation period and jump distance when transitioning from hard to soft ground.

In the era of Industry 4.0, the Internet of Things (IoT) has become a cornerstone, with edge computing and mesh networking driving the evolution of smart manufacturing. However, the successful integration of IoT systems relies heavily on the efficient management of edge devices, particularly through timely firmware updates. To address this challenge, researchers have developed the firmware update request protocol (FURP) to facilitate real-time, over-the-air updates for mesh networks, utilizing the inherent features of the Internet of Things. To gauge the performance of FURP, this paper presents a comprehensive evaluation conducted on a large-scale production-level mesh network, involving real-time firmware updates for 100 nodes. The results demonstrate the practicality and effectiveness of both the FURP protocol and the mesh network in supporting scalable, manageable large-scale smart manufacturing.

We've studied the transition many-body localization (MBL) using the extended Heisenberg spin chain, employing a configuration space propagator derived from the continuous-time exact diagonalization method. By examining the decay properties of this propagator, we can identify MBL and volume-law entanglement growth. Notably, the size of the localized region in the critical state follows a power-law pattern, consistent with the size of the active Hilbert space, and this power-law exponent is found to be identical to the multifractal exponent governing the size of the typical MBL eigenstate support. Furthermore, the spin chain's localized regime displays volume-law entanglement growth, and the spin chain chain's localized regime displays volume-law entanglement growth, and the spin chain chain's localized regime displays volume-law entanglement growth, and the spin chain chain's localized regime displays volume-law entanglement growth, and the spin chain chain's localized regime displays volume-law entanglement growth, and the spin chain chain's localized regime displays volume-law entanglement growth, and the spin chain chain's localized regime displays volume-law entanglement growth, and the spin chain chain's localized regime displays volume-law entanglement growth, and the spin chain chain's localized regime displays volume-law entanglement growth, and the spin chain chain's localized regime displays volume-law entanglement growth, and the spin chain chain's localized regime displays volume-law entanglement growth, and the spin chain chain's

In real-world situations, it's often necessary to locate multiple objects simultaneously within a large image, but doing so can be a time-consuming task. To streamline this process, users can provide feedback by eliminating incorrect possibilities, but doing so may be frustrating if the number of objects needs to be located is large. To address these issues, this paper proposes an efficient search method that allows users to remove unwanted options within a certain budget, constraining the total number of eliminations allowed. The proposed algorithm strategically allocates the budget to remove the most informative options, ensuring the search process remains efficient. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through experiments conducted on a comprehensive dataset.

Machine and quantum learning algorithms face a shared vulnerability to adversarial examples, which can mislead them into making incorrect classifications with seemingly negligible alterations to the original data. In the realm of quantum machine learning, where quantum circuits serve as the universal function approximators, researchers have discovered that adversarial examples can be achieved by subtracting the gradient of the loss function from the input. Furthermore, they have shown that these adversarial examples remain effective across various quantum classifiers and can even be created using classical data. In the process, a quantum version of the strong convexity was also established.

We demonstrate that Steklov eigenvalues of nearly spherical domains are positive polynomial functions of the coefficients that define the nearly spherical perturbations. This discovery leads to the conclusion that each positive integer appears as a multiplicity in the spectrum of such domain eigenvalues. The result also enables us to calculate explicit bounds for the eigenvalues.

Conformance checking is the process of comparing observed behavior to the predefined process model.  Observations, or traces, are often compared to ensure they follow the defined process model, which is typically done using alignments.  However, many real-life cases involve only partial matches of process activities, which are not addressed by current alignment-based conformance checking methods.  To address this gap, we propose new methods for analyzing the fragments of traces and develop two approaches: analyzing trace fragments within the context of their full process (infix alignments) and those that come after the fragment (postfix alignments).  We establish that these approaches provide different but complementary views of trace conformity and outline their benefits and drawbacks.  To illustrate this, we provide examples of where each approach excels and provide a performance comparison between them.

Radio propagation prediction in cellular networks is typically done using either ray-tracing or empirical modeling methods. Ray-tracing is highly accurate but computationally expensive, while empirical models are faster but rely on simplifications and may not be accurate enough. This paper proposes a deep learning-based approach that uses convolutional neural networks to create a mapping between a simple empirical model input and the radiation pattern produced by a complex ray-tracing simulation. The proposed model, called ConvNet, takes the input of a simple empirical model and outputs an approximation of the ray-tracing produced pattern. The accuracy of ConvNet is evaluated by comparing the differences between its output and the ray-tracing produced pattern, and the results show that ConvNet is able to accurately approximate the ray-tracing produced pattern, and is faster than both ray-tracing and a standard empirical model.

We define a precise meaning for temporal planning and verify the correctness of widely used planning validation methods through formal verification. By using the Isar proof assistant and a formal model of actions, we ensure that these validation methods meet the planning model, which resolves issues in PDDL where invalid actions can cause planning failures. We discovered that standard validation methods are not entirely accurate, and we present a revised validation method that satisfies the planning model, accompanied by a formal proof of its correctness. Moreover, we examine how various formalisms for specifying temporal constraints impact the planning model and discuss the potential for incorporating more expressive temporal logic into planning.

Power system expansion planning models are crucial in determining the most cost-effective system expansion. These models are typically built using optimization techniques that rely on various uncertain parameters. The impact of parameter uncertainty on model outcomes can be significant, but this is often overlooked. The sensitivity of power system models to key parameters is investigated in this study, with a particular focus on the cost of system expansion, the capacity of new generation, and the capacity of new transmission lines. The research involves the use of multiple models, including the MISO summer model and the EnergyScenarios model, to examine the sensitivity of system expansion to parameters such as capacity factors, fuel costs, and transmission losses. The results indicate that the sensitivity of system expansion to these parameters can be substantial, and that the optimal system expansion may vary significantly under different parameter assumptions. The study also reveals that the sensitivity of system expansion to parameters such as fuel costs and transmission losses is not uniform across all regions, and that the sensitivity of system expansion to parameters such as capacity factors and fuel costs is influenced by the level of transmission capacity. The research has significant implications for policy makers and system operators, and that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that that

This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for the Vlasov-Poisson and the Keller-Segel models within confined areas, under specified boundary conditions that include a reflective surface for the former and a zero value at the boundary for the latter. Utilizing the method of characteristics, the paper leverages the method of steps to demonstrate the short-term well-posedness of these systems, and employs the way of steps argument in conjunction with the heat equation's properties for the paper at short-term for Keller-Segel model. Subsequently, the paper uses the method of continuation in time to prove the global well-posedness for the Vlasov-Poisson model, and for the Keller-Segel model, the paper uses the method of continuation in time to prove the global well-posedness by iteratively applying the results from the method of steps argument.

When developers work on large projects, they frequently encounter the need to
locate specific concepts within an extensive codebase. However, they often struggle
to identify the appropriate search terms to utilize when performing a concept-
oriented search. To address this issue, we propose a technique that assists
developers in identifying effective search terms by analyzing past search logs.
Our approach recommends a set of optimized search terms derived from similar
concepts within the codebase, thereby enhancing the efficiency of concept
location. The efficacy of our solution is demonstrated through user studies,
which show that it successfully suggests relevant search terms and is easily
adoptable by developers.

Researchers have discovered that ultrasonic waves can significantly alter the mechanical and flow properties of colloidal gels. By applying acoustic energy, they can temporarily weaken the gel's structure, making it easier to manipulate and process. This phenomenon is referred to as rheo-acoustics and it offers a versatile method for controlling the properties of colloidal gels. Our study reveals that ultrasonic vibrations can reduce a gel's stiffness, as well as modify its ability to recover from deformation. Moreover, we found that the application of acoustic energy can also significantly impact the flow behavior of the gel, as well as the time it takes for the gel to recover its original properties after being disturbed. This unique response is influenced by the characteristics of the ultrasonic waves, such as frequency and intensity, as well as the specific composition of the colloidal gel. Our research demonstrates that ultrasonic vibrations can effectively disrupt the gel's structure, causing a more pronounced and long-lasting transition to a softer state. This discovery opens up a wide range of possibilities for the manipulation and processing of colloidal gels, and it has the potential to revolutionize the way we understand and utilize these materials.

This research investigates the validity of the Collatz conjecture, offering a novel proof that the sequence defined by f(x) generates a descending spiral, ultimately converging to 1 for all natural numbers x.

To effectively understand the contents of scientific research papers, it is crucial to grasp their specialized terminology and apply it to automated tasks like classification. However, research paper classification systems often rely on keyword-based methods that fail to consider the actual meaning of these keywords. To rectify this issue, we propose the use of knowledge-based approaches, specifically focusing on semantic relationships between mathematical entities in paper formulas. By establishing connections between abstract concepts and their real-world counterparts in mathematical expressions, we can enhance the interpretability of automated classification systems in the field of mathematics.

In the context of stable matching, we examine the dynamics of the Deferred Acceptance algorithm when agents have the option to choose which proposals to submit, focusing on how this affects outcomes in a two-sided matching market. We demonstrate that when agents have the choice of which proposals to make in a bipartite matching market, outcomes from the $r$-round execution of the Deferred Acceptance algorithm fall within the Shapley-Schvaneveldt order, a concept that ranks match outcomes by their quality. We further show that if the number of allowed proposals per agent ($r$) is equal to or greater than the market size, all possible match outcomes will be optimal for the involved agents. We also explore the implications of this finding, including its use in understanding how to optimize the execution of the Deferred Acceptance algorithm in kidney exchange programs.

To assess a summary's effectiveness, a metric must consider its content,
coherence, and grammatical correctness. While a metric based on a cross-encoder
can evaluate content and coherence, it falls short in detecting repetition and
omission errors. In this study, a novel metric called SummScore is proposed,
which integrates multiple features, including a cross-encoder and a BERT model,
to evaluate a summary's quality. This new approach successfully detects
duplications and omissions, making it a comprehensive evaluation tool for
summarization. SummScore has been tested on the TED, ROCStories, and CNN/DailyMail
datasets and consistently achieved superior performance over existing metrics.

We introduce and analyze an innovative signal recovery technique based on the expectation-maximization algorithm, which is adapted for implementation in a parallel and iterative manner. This algorithm enhances signal reconstruction from highly redundant data obtained through the application of a signal-specific transformation, such as a dictionary or a graph-based mapping. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm in a mathematical framework, providing a proof of convergence and a bound on the expected number of iterations required for recovery. Additionally, we conduct a comprehensive simulation study, which reveals that this algorithm outperforms an existing method in a relevant benchmark scenario.

This research presents BEVFusion, a pioneering and robust approach to incorporating vision-based inputs from LiDAR and cameras in the LiDARBird360 dataset for 360-degree vehicle classification. Unlike traditional methods that convert data into images, BEVFusion directly fuses the integrated bird's-eye view feature maps of each modality through cross-attention mechanisms. A key component of the framework is a selective fusion module that selectively combines the features from both modality and the bird's-eye view, enhancing the representation of objects that are only visible in the camera channel. The proposed framework boasts a high level of efficiency, with its parameter count and floating point operations being comparable to the state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, BEVFusion surpasses the performance of the current best methods in both accuracy and robustness, demonstrating remarkable stability across the day and night cycles.

We have derived an effective theory for incompressible fluid turbulence, focusing on the dissipation range, by incorporating thermal fluctuations. This is achieved through a systematic expansion of the fluid's coarse-grained hydrodynamics, which is then used to investigate the behavior of turbulent fluids at a scale smaller than the largest eddies. We have calculated the leading-order effects of thermal fluctuations and found that they are dominated by an enhanced dissipation term, which is independent of temperature. This result is consistent with previous numerical studies and theoretical predictions. We have also found that the leading-order effects of thermal fluctuations are suppressed by a factor of the Reynolds number, which is large in most astrophysical and atmospheric flows. This suggests that thermal fluctuations may be negligible in most astrophysical and atmospheric turbulent flows.

The dynamics of laser propagation through a liquid medium have been numerically studied, with a focus on understanding the formation of diffraction gratings. The research involved analyzing the behavior of a 1064 nm Nd:YAG laser in various liquids, including water, ethanol, and methanol, under different pulse durations. The results showed that the grating period varied significantly with pulse duration, ranging from 10 micrometers to 1 millimeter. The study identified the key factors influencing grating formation, including the role of heat transfer and the absorption coefficient of the liquid. The research also revealed the complex interplay between multiple absorption peaks and the resulting grating patterns. The findings have significant implications for understanding and controlling the behavior of lasers in liquid media, with potential applications in various fields, including material processing and biomedical applications.

In the field of software design, there's a growing need for a structured approach,
which can be automatically extracted from developers' comments in source code control systems.
These systems contain valuable information about design decisions,
which can be mined and used for various purposes, such as automatic generation of design documentation.
However, a significant challenge lies in the fact that developers' comments are often written in natural language,
which can be ambiguous and unclear.
To address this issue, we propose a new approach to defining the structure of design decisions,
focusing on their role as a cause for decisions rather than their content.
By doing so, we can achieve more accurate extraction of design decision metadata,
resulting in more useful documentation and design support tools.

As stream and event data grows exponentially, organizations are increasingly dependent on business analytics to extract actionable insights from data. However, current data querying and mining tools are inadequate to handle the deluge of data, while big data analytics systems lack the capability to process real-time data streams. H-STREAM is a comprehensive data querying and mining platform that bridges this gap, enabling the seamless integration of data mining tools and data streaming capabilities. This paper details the architecture of H-STREAM, its core components, and its ability to build scalable data querying pipelines. Furthermore, the paper showcases a case study where H-STREAM was used to analyze data from a large-scale social media platform, generating valuable insights into user behavior and trends.

We've calculated production cross-sections for a specific group of Higgs-like scalars, consisting of a doublet and singlet, as well as the pseudoscalar partner of the top and bottom quarks, within the most general top coloron model. In this framework, we've established that the production of a bottom and the pseudoscalar partner through the fusion of a Higgs field and a photon is the primary mechanism for single bottom partner production at the Large Hadron Collider. In contrast, a detailed investigation of top, anti-top quark pair production in combination with a photon revealed that these interactions are negligible. We've also found that, in single top and anti-top partner production involving a photon, the production rates are largely influenced by the mass of the coloron, with the Higgs production rate being the primary determinant of the production rate of a top and the scalar or pseudoscalar partner.

In knowledge base question answering, machine translates queries using QA data from a knowledge base into related queries using QB data from a knowledge base. However, current methods rely on word alignments between the two data sets, which are limited to vocabulary from the alignment model. As a result, unknown elements in QB queries cannot be mapped to corresponding elements in QB queries, causing a decline in overall system performance. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a new method for handling elements in knowledge base queries that involves predicting alignments between the queries. By using this method, the system can successfully map corresponding elements in knowledge base queries, thereby improving overall system performance. By incorporating this method, the system achieved an increase in F1 score of 0.40 and an accuracy of 0.10 on the CQA dataset.

This paper introduces venue analytics, a straightforward alternative to the traditional citation-based metrics, which often suffer from biases against early career researchers. Unlike these metrics, venue analytics assesses the quality of a paper's venue, taking into account the diverse factors that influence its citation count, such as the paper's field, year of publication, and conference prestige. By focusing on the venue rather than the individual author, venue analytics provides a more accurate reflection of the paper's quality and impact.

This research focuses on the verification of neural networks, with a particular emphasis on their applications in control and safety-critical systems. The presentation will comprise two distinct parts, each exploring distinct aspects of the topic. The first part will review the current state of neural network verification, encompassing the formal description of various neural network types, control systems, and the types of properties that can be verified. The second part will delve into specific techniques for analyzing and verifying feed-forward neural networks, encompassing particular approaches and their respective applications. The third part will examine the validation of deep feed-forward neural networks, focusing on the limitations of existing verification methods and the potential applications of neural networks in control systems, particularly in the context of safety-critical systems. The fourth and fifth parts will discuss the limitations of representing feed-forward neural networks, focusing on the implications of these limitations for control applications. The sixth part will explore the current state of feed-forward neural network verification, highlighting the types of properties that can be verified and the challenges associated with the verification of feed-forward neural networks, particularly in the context of safety-critical systems.

We've developed a clustering technique that builds on the concept of dendrograms, similar to traditional methods, yet creates more complex, overlapping relationships between data points. Given any choice function that determines the next step in the clustering process, our algorithm generates unique clustering structures, or overlaps, which can be represented as directed weighted graphs, and proves to be efficient with a computational complexity of O(n^2). Furthermore, the weighted graphs created by this method have distinct properties, such as the ability for any choice function to produce a clustering structure equivalent to cutting a choice-invariant dendrogram, and the ability for any such equivalence to be represented as a choice-invariant dendrogram, which even has the ability to create overlapping relationships equivalent to those of our algorithm. Our study also demonstrates that selecting the next step in the clustering process can be based solely on the local submatrix of the distance matrix, which contains the distances between the points being considered, and unlike traditional methods, this distance matrix does not need to be symmetric or complete to create clustering structures, although the distribution of edge weights in the resulting graph depends on the matrix's completeness and symmetry.

A recently developed low-rank approach called tensor ring decomposition has gained attention for its effectiveness in handling low-quality images and videos. However, traditional streaming algorithms for completing tensor ring data struggle to process high-resolution visual data efficiently due to their high memory demands. To address this limitation, a novel method called PTRA is introduced, which enables the efficient reconstruction of a tensor ring sequence in real-time. By breaking down the sequence into overlapping segments and tracking individual frames, PTRA significantly reduces the computation and memory needs. To further enhance its efficiency, PTRA incorporates a low-cost update mechanism that only calculates the differences between consecutive patches. The proposed method has been extensively tested on various types of image degradation, including motion blur, defocus, and salt and pepper noise, with impressive results demonstrating its superiority over existing techniques.

It is demonstrated that for any classical Weyl group W, and any degree 2 braiding N, the associated Nichols algebra is contained within an orthogonal or symplectic field with the same characteristic as W, specifically within either GO(n,F) or GSp(n,F) where n equals the rank of W, with the field F being either of characteristic zero or a prime p greater than the degree of W.

Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, which is characterized by inertial waves, is a subject of significant interest in geophysical and astrophysical flows. The primary goal of this research is to conduct direct numerical simulations of fully developed turbulence in three-dimensional rotating flow. The simulations reveal distinct features, with large-scale motions initially driving turbulence and transferring energy to smaller scales. Notably, these smaller scales exhibit a Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum with a k^-3 relationship.

We investigate a specific graph coloring problem, focusing on determining the minimum number of colors needed for an undirected graph, with the constraint that the subgraph formed by nodes of the largest color class must be a maximum-weight independent set, with a given weight function. An iterative graph transformation is proposed to solve this problem, with the aim of finding a coloring where the largest class uses the minimum number of colors. It is shown that this color number is either the same as the graph's chromatic number, or greater by at most one. Key aspects of this problem include analyzing the behavior of the transformation, proving the proposed algorithm's correctness, and exploring its time complexity.

This research examines the impact of a magnetic field on electrically modulated single-layer graphene, focusing on its thermodynamic properties. The modulation's spatial characteristics are adjustable through electric fields applied perpendicularly. The researchers investigated the electrical modulated graphene in the presence of up to three Landau levels to analyze how the filling factor and modulation parameters affect various thermodynamic properties. Theoretical models based on upland and interlandau transitions are used to describe the system's behavior. Theoretical predictions reveal that entropy, specific heat, and susceptibility are influenced by upland transitions, whereas specific heat and susceptibility are affected by interlandau transitions. The findings indicate that entropy and specific heat demonstrate oscillatory patterns in response to changes in the modulation wave number, filling factor, and wave phase.

The study aimed to understand the evolution of this emission at 30 MHz and its connection to stellar activity. The results revealed that the emission from both stars remained stable over a 10-day period, with no significant changes. The brightness of the emission was found to be inversely related to the stellar rotation speed, with one star exhibiting brighter emission when rotating faster. The study also discovered that the emission from one star was beamed towards Earth, while the other was not. By integrating 3D human avatars with neural rendering techniques, we can create a dynamic model that enables virtual avatars to interact seamlessly with real-world environments. In contrast to traditional approaches that solely focus on appearance, our unified framework combines body pose, facial expressions, and model texture into a single, cohesive system. The ANR system leverages an articulated neural body renderer paired with neural texture and geometry fields to accurately capture detailed avatars in various poses and lighting conditions. Furthermore, our system incorporates a unified training strategy that synchronizes these components through a joint optimization process. The ANR system's capabilities are demonstrated through virtual avatar interactions in real-world settings, as well as its application in digital human production.

In the field of Computer Vision, data augmentation techniques are used to enhance the robustness of models by simulating various environmental conditions. While beneficial, these techniques can also inadvertently cause models to become vulnerable to attacks by introducing patterns that are easily exploitable. This research explores the impact of novel, intense data transformations on both human perception and machine learning models. Our study reveals that machines and humans respond differently to these extreme transformations, with humans retaining recognition abilities in scenarios where machines fail. This finding underscores the necessity for a more accurate understanding of how machines process visual information, especially in relation to human perception.

The Askey-Wilson algebra has a connection to the Chern-Simons theory when using quantum parameters q and q^3, leading to a representation of the algebra that uses a 3-tensor. This representation is used to create a link between the algebra and a one-point function in the Chern-Simons theory, which in turn allows the link invariants defined by the algebra to correspond to Wilson loop expectations. Additionally, it is shown that the q-deformed Hecke algebra's representation can be embedded in both the Chern-Simons theory and the Askey-Wilson algebra.

We investigate the properties of two-dimensional frustrated antiferromagnets with weakly-coupled trimer lattices. Utilizing the exact solution to the 2D classical Ising model, our findings reveal that at low temperatures, large-scale ordering occurs, specifically a periodic arrangement of trimer units. This periodic structure is confirmed by performing a quantum simulation with the full-cluster quantum Monte Carlo method, showing that the system undergoes a quantum phase transition at a specific spin-ising exponent. This transition is characterized by power-law correlations and quantum fluctuations, specifically at a specific exponent value. This transition is further verified by measuring the system's susceptibility, showing a minimum at a specific point and a temperature-dependent behavior. This behavior is also consistent with the predictions of mean-field theory, showing that the system undergoes a transition at a specific point and exhibits a specific type of ordering.

Pre-trained language models have become the foundation for numerous natural language processing tasks, with prompt-based methods emerging as a leading approach for next-token prediction. These prompts, consisting of a template and fill-in-the-blank text, enable models to learn task parameters from pre-trained representations. However, the effectiveness of prompts relies heavily on the quality of the prompt design and training data. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages meta-learning to adapt language models to a range of prompts and training data templates. Our method, called PromptBase, creates a database of prompts and training data, allowing models to tune their parameters to each entry. The resulting meta-tuned model can then be used to generate prompt-based representations for any task, even those with pre-existing language model solutions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PromptBase on three language understanding benchmarks, showing that it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, including inductive transfer and few-shot learning.

In this study, we investigate the possibility of electroweak baryogenesis in the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM framework under the assumption of a first-order phase transition. Our research indicates that under these conditions, the phase transition is inherently smooth unless there is a substantial off-diagonal term in the Higgsino mass matrix. We further find that the parameter space allowing for a detectable phase transition is relatively limited, with many constraints arising from various factors, including Higgs data, flavor data, and dark matter data. Our findings show that the available parameter space is further restricted by the Higgs data and flavor data, with flavor data being the primary factor in many cases. Our analysis also reveals that the remaining parameter space can be probed by direct dark matter searches and future collider experiments.

We introduce a novel approach to diagnosing photometric redshifts, where a high-z Sudoku algorithm is utilized to pinpoint potential outliers in the redshift catalog. By cross-referencing spectroscopic redshifts with Sudoku classifications, we can gauge the reliability of photometric redshifts. We applied this method to 14 galaxies at a photometric redshift of z_p=2.85, which possess spectroscopic redshifts that are either incorrect or absent. Utilizing Subaru's Bessell filters and Subaru/Subaru Bessell filter data, we obtained a z_sx estimate for 10 galaxies, which resulted in 7 accurate results and 3 potential candidates. Furthermore, we analyzed the performance of the z_p and z_sx catalogs in terms of their ability to detect Lyman-alpha emission and identify galaxies that are obscured by dust. Our analysis revealed that the Sudoku-based catalog has a higher detection rate of 60% for Lyman-alpha emitters, which is an improvement over the 40% detection rate of the z_p catalog. Additionally, the Sudoku-based catalog has a higher detection rate of 60% for dusty galaxies, which is an improvement over the 40% detection rate of the z_p catalog.

The $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnetic lattice on a triangular structure is a model of interest in condensed matter physics, exhibiting various phases such as geometric frustration, a columnar dimer phase, and Luttinger-Lieb liquids. Recent research has identified the columnar dimer phase in certain materials, but the emergence of a Luttinger-Liquid phase remains unconfirmed. Our study focuses on investigating the possibility of a Luttinger-Liquid phase in a similar system, by performing numerical simulations using the density-matrix renormalization group method. We find that the system undergoes dynamic transitions at two critical temperatures, $T_c^*$ and $T_{cf}$, which mark the onset of dynamic signatures associated with the Luttinger-Liquid phase and the classical columnar Dimer phase transition, respectively. Our findings suggest that the system undergoes a phase transition at $T_c^*$, which is a clear indicator of a quantum phase transition.

The confinement-deconfinement shift in $SU(3)-$Higgs theory is examined through the behavior of the Polyline loop. Researchers employed Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the large-$N$ limit of the two-color $SU(N)$ and $SU(N+1)$ Higgs theories, specifically at $N=\infty$. The study revealed that the large-$N$ limit of the Polyline loop differs between these theories, with the latter exhibiting a distinct form. Additionally, researchers found that the deconfinement phase transition in $SU(3)-$Higgs theory is influenced by the Higgs field, resulting in a change from a first-order to a crossover phase as the Higgs coupling increases.

Cr$_{2}$Al exhibits a unique crystal structure, with two distinct chromium sublattices, A and B, that are arranged in an SDArS pattern along with the aluminum layer. At a temperature of 205 K, this material undergoes an antiferromagnetic phase transition, characterized by the magnetic moment of approximately 0.7 $\mu_{B}$ for both sublattices B and A, but they are oriented in opposite directions. Our research, utilizing neutron powder diffraction, reveals that the magnetic sublattices A and B are positioned perpendicular to the crystallographic c-axis, specifically along the a-axis. Additionally, our findings indicate that the magnetic interactions within sublattice A and B are similar and primarily consist of strong in-plane antiferromagnetic coupling and weak interplane interactions.

A novel kinetic model is developed for rarefied monatomic gas flows, incorporating the effects of weakly attractive intermolecular potentials through velocity-dependent collision frequency. We derive an analytical expression for collision frequency as a function of relative particle velocity using the kinetic theory of Born-Green-Yvon. The proposed model consists of one continuity equation and one energy transport equation, representing the conservation of mass and energy, respectively. This kinetic model is validated through comparisons with results from molecular dynamics simulations and the Shock-Standing-Wave experiment, yielding satisfactory agreement with numerical and experimental data.

Semantic parsers translate natural language sentences into logical forms, facilitating a connection between human language and computer systems. Traditional semantic parsers rely on large datasets annotated with special markers and templates, which are difficult to obtain. We introduce novel methods for training high-performance parsers using minimal annotations. This involves annotating logical forms with context-specific details, allowing parsers to learn and refine their understanding. We develop two annotation types - free-form and constrained, each offering distinct benefits. The unconstrained annotation style yields the most accurate results, while the constrained style is easier to manage. We also introduce a novel training approach, ConfiNe, which adjusts the amount of context information used in training to achieve optimal performance. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing approaches, enabling training with a fraction of the data required by traditional parsers.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will rely heavily on precise jet measurements and particle identification in high-energy collisions. To support these measurements, the futureEIC-FST will utilize a hybrid tracking detector, incorporating a forward section that spans from 1.5 to 100 times the high-energy collisions angle. This forward detector, designed for future electron-ion collisions, will be developed by a global collaboration of experimental physicists. A recent development phase has seen the selection of a new silicon sensor technology, which is now being optimized for production. This paper will outline the design and performance goals of the future tracking detector, along with the current progress and plans for developing the new silicon sensors.

The magnetic fields of cool stars are primarily generated by a dynamo process, which is influenced by convection and rotation. The resulting magnetic field configuration is usually axisymmetric and predominantly poloidal. Observations of cool stars often reveal a dipolar magnetic field structure, but the radial field gradient has not been directly observed. In this study, we investigate the magnetic field structure of the cool K5V star HD58260, which has a predominantly dipolar configuration. Using high-resolution spectropolarimetry, we analyze the magnetic signatures of two emission lines, which are formed in the stellar atmosphere's upper layers. The analysis reveals that the radial field gradient in HD58260 is consistent with a dipolar magnetic field structure, which is confirmed by our results. The radial field gradient is found to be more pronounced in the emission lines compared to Fe I and Cr I lines, which are formed in the photosphere. exemplified through its equivalence to a differential operator,

A recent discovery has revealed that the H30 $\alpha$ line at a wavelength of 870 $\mu$m can be observed in galaxies, which is highly sensitive to the mass of stars being formed. A study of the galaxy NGC 5253, observed with the ALMA telescope, has provided new insights into its star-forming regions. The data collected from NGC 5253, specifically in its rest-frame mid-infrared range, has been analyzed and compared with other star-forming tracers. A total of 10 distinct emission lines were detected, which allowed for the determination of the redshift of the galaxy to be 0.0322 $\pm$ 0.0001. The data also showed that the H30 $\alpha$ line is a reliable indicator of star formation, which is consistent with theoretical predictions. A comparison of NGC 5253's data with other star-forming tracers revealed that the H30 $\alpha$ line is more sensitive to younger stars, which is an advantage in studying the star formation history of galaxies. The data also showed that the H30 $\alpha$ line is less affected by dust extinction, which is an advantage in studying galaxies with high levels of dust.
